inline.s: Here I set forth the instructions on how to practise Buddha-recitation given by Master Shandao and Master Yongming, both incarnations of Amitābha Buddha. Those who advocate reciting with a scattered mind may hold up their own words and actions for comparison and see how they are deceiving sentient beings.
Master Shandao taught:
With a single-pointed mind
recite solely the name of Amitābha Buddha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, heedless of the duration, never abandoning it thought after thought
(an unbroken succession of thoughts)
— such a one is named the karma of right concentration,
in accord with that Buddha's
(Amitābha Buddha's)
vow
Unbroken succession brings rebirth.
If one can keep
thought after thought unbroken until the very end of life,
then ten of ten are reborn and a hundred of a hundred.
May all people reflect on this well: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must
rouse the will and master oneself
(spurring oneself on and holding oneself in check),
never letting the effort flag by day or night;
when the previous thought comes to an end,
the next thought is immediately born.
To forever relish the unconditioned joy of the Dharma, even up to the attainment of Buddhahood — how wondrous a thing it is!
Master Yongming taught:
If words and actions are out of keeping,
and the power of faith is faint,
one who lacks
a mind of unbroken succession of thoughts
but rather a mind interrupted again and again
(the thought of recitation is cut off again and again by wandering thoughts — this is scattered-mind recitation),
and
resting in this indolence,
hopes for rebirth at the moment of death, yet, veiled by his karma, may hardly encounter his good spiritual friend
(it is feared he will not meet the great teacher of virtue who can sustain his right mindfulness at death),
and as the wind and fire press on him,
right mindfulness is not accomplished
Why so?
The present life is the cause, death is the fruit;
the cause must be made solid, and then the fruit will not be false. If one would bring about
the ten thoughts at the moment of death,
(that is, to accomplish the unbroken succession of ten thoughts at death),
then one must
make ready the bridge beforehand
(that is, to prepare fully in advance),
gather together merit and dedicate it to that time
(dedicate it to the moment of death),
and as long as the thoughts do not fall short
(i.e., the succession of thoughts is unbroken),
then there is nothing to worry about.
Question: An article says: “Master Shandao, in his Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra, says: ‘
From the contemplation of the sun down through the thirteenth contemplation is called concentrated good; the three kinds of merit and the nine grades are called scattered good.’
The three kinds of merit and even the nine grades
— even rebirth in the highest rank of the highest grade is scattered good.
Thus we know that
if you have genuine faith and a sincere vow, scattered-mind recitation will absolutely, one hundred percent, lead to rebirth.
” Is this so?

Answer: The logic of that passage is: “The three kinds of merit and even the nine grades — even rebirth in the highest rank of the highest grade — are scattered good”; scattered-mind recitation is scattered good, and so “scattered-mind recitation will absolutely one hundred percent lead to rebirth.” If we follow this logic, then since “even rebirth in the highest rank of the highest grade is scattered good,” that highest rebirth likewise is all through scattered-mind recitation! This is a complete distortion of “scattered good” in the Contemplation Sutra. The “scattered” of scattered good is spoken in contrast to the “concentrated” of the sustained, focused, and subtle contemplation-aim of the first thirteen contemplations (see
the Annotation on the Lowest-Grade Lowest-Birth Chapter of the Contemplation Sutra
) that is sustained and single-minded toward a subtle object of contemplation. Whereas the “scattered” of scattered-mind recitation means that one wanders in wild thoughts while reciting. Therefore,
these two “scattered” do not carry the same meaning

In the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra, Master Shandao also lays great stress on single-minded recitation. If scattered-mind recitation were scattered good, why would Master Shandao in that very same writing still teach that “
single-minded recitation is the true proper practice
”? Master Shandao says:

“Practice, however, is of two kinds: the first is proper practice, and the second is mixed practice. As for proper practice, one who relies solely upon the practices given in the rebirth sutras is called a practitioner of proper practice. What does that mean?
With a single mind,
single-heartedly read and recite this Contemplation Sutra, the Amitābha Sutra, the Immeasurable Life Sutra, and the like;
with single-minded focus
contemplate, observe, and recollect the adornment of the two rewards of that land. If one bows, then
with a single mind
single-heartedly bow to that Buddha; if one recites aloud, then
with a single mind single-heartedly call upon that Buddha
; if one praises and offers, then with a single mind single-heartedly praise and offer.
This is called proper practice
With a single mind, single-heartedly recollect the name of Amitābha Buddha
, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, heedless of the duration,
the one who never abandons it thought after thought
(never interrupted by wandering thoughts)
— this is named
the karma of right concentration
(For the commentary see
the Pure Land Teachings of Master Shandao
.) If scattered-mind recitation were scattered good, why would Master Shandao, in that same book, still treat single-minded recitation as a special topic, and even hold it up as
the karma of right concentration
! Therefore,

Master Shandao's instructions on scattered good and his instructions on single-minded recitation in the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra together prove that scattered-mind recitation is not scattered good, because scattered-mind recitation is not proper practice; single-minded recitation is the proper practice!
Master Shandao says:

“Practice, however, is of two kinds: the first is proper practice, and the second is mixed practice. As for proper practice, one who relies solely upon the practices given in the rebirth sutras is called a practitioner of proper practice. What does that mean?
If one recites aloud, then
with a single mind single-heartedly call upon that Buddha
this is called the proper practice

In fact, “if you have genuine faith and a sincere vow, scattered-mind recitation will absolutely one hundred percent lead to rebirth” is utterly fallacious. Where is there anyone of genuine faith and sincere vow who still recites with a scattered mind? Those who recite with a scattered mind do so precisely because they shrink from hardship and pain, and therefore act against the instruction of the Buddha and the patriarchs — this is precisely the concrete expression of faith that is not genuine and vows that are not sincere. Therefore, those who recite with a scattered mind surely do not have genuine faith and sincere vows. The very situation of “scattered-mind recitation together with genuine faith and sincere vows” simply does not exist; it is a false proposition, just as there is no such thing as a brave soldier who quails on the battlefield. (See the discussion above.)

Question: An article says: “Venerable Miaolian, who passed away a few years ago and who, in twenty years, practised the Pratyutpanna Samādhi ten times, made his forty-ninth great vow: that even scattered-mind recitation can bring rebirth.” Is this so?

Answer: As far as I know, Venerable Miaolian's forty-ninth great vow was: “Whoever has seen my face, heard my teaching, or even heard my name, I shall deliver them all to be reborn together in the Western Pure Land; if in this life they fail to be reborn there, I shall surely return again to teach and deliver them, until they are reborn in the West.” It was not: “Even scattered-mind recitation can bring rebirth.” You may go online and verify.

If someone truly makes a forty-ninth great vow of “even scattered-mind recitation can bring rebirth,” then he is slandering the Buddha and is accusing Amitābha Buddha of not coming to fetch the beings who recite with a scattered mind. Such a person, who does not understand the Dharma himself, yet so arrogantly makes such a forty-ninth great vow, wishing to rise above Amitābha Buddha, the King among Buddhas!
[King among Buddhas] The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha Buddha says:

“Amitābha Buddha's light is pure and free from stain, without flaw or diminution. The light of Amitābha Buddha is lovely and surpasses the brightness of the sun and moon by a hundred thousand millions of times. It is the brightest among all Buddhas' lights, the finest among lights, the most majestic among lights, the most swift and good among lights,
the King among all Buddhas,
the most honoured of lights, the brightest and most immeasurable of lights.”
In fact,
at the moment of the death of every single being, Amitābha Buddha is there to welcome him,
including those who have recited with a scattered mind.
It is only that beings without right mindfulness at the point of death cannot see it, and so they follow their own wandering thoughts and are reborn according to their karma.
Therefore, one must hold right mindfulness at death before he can see Amitābha Buddha come to welcome him and, following the Buddha, be reborn in the Western Pure Land.
On this principle, Master Zhongfeng, honoured as the ancient Buddha of Jiangnan, taught in the “Three Sessions of Remembrance”:
Although it is said that Amitābha gathers in beings for their rebirth, one must believe
it is only one's own mind that manifests it,
that is,
the mutual resonance of the mind and the Buddha,
and that in the end
(after all)
it is not obtained from outside

[Only the self-manifestation of one's own mind] Amitābha Buddha's coming to welcome (gather in) beings is solely the manifestation of one's own mind; this is because of the mutual resonance of sympathetic response, and is not something obtained from outside. Therefore only those with right mindfulness at death can see the Buddha come, while the others around them cannot. Those beings who are deluded at death, because their minds are turbid and confused and they lack the sense of right mindfulness (the unbroken succession of ten thoughts), naturally will not have Amitābha Buddha's coming to welcome them appear in their minds, and so they cannot see the Buddha come —
not because Amitābha Buddha did not come to welcome them
The Sutra of Immeasurable Life spoken by the Buddha says:
“That land does not turn anyone away
(the Pure Land refuses no being rebirth there)
but is drawn along by nature
(those beings who do not attain rebirth in the Pure Land naturally follow their own dying wandering thoughts and are born into the six realms)
Therefore, rebirth or not depends entirely on whether one has right mindfulness at death
(the unbroken succession of ten thoughts at death)
This is why
Master Shandao and Master Yongming, both avatars of Amitābha Buddha, earnestly teach again and again:
one must accomplish the unbroken succession of ten thoughts at death
(see
the Eighteenth Vow
article)
. This, after all, is the instruction of Amitābha Buddha himself!
[Mutual resonance of sympathetic response] The response of sentient beings and the response of Amitābha Buddha interpenetrate each other.
[Those beings who do not attain rebirth in the Pure Land naturally follow their dying wandering thoughts and are reborn in the six realms] On this matter, Master Lianchi taught:
Those who are deluded at death

, because all their lives they indulged their wandering thoughts, never cultivating right mindfulness, and their minds were mostly scattered and confused. At the time when the warmth of the body is about to leave
(the moment when the four elements break apart)

, the deeds of a whole life all appear before them, and their minds tremble with terror and their movements become frantic. The one who should descend to hell sees the mountain of knives and the forest of swords as a garden. The one who should fall among the animals takes the womb of a horse and the belly of a donkey to be a hall. Even those who have done good and should be reborn among humans or gods cannot escape loving and hating their parents. Even the lesser sages of the lesser vehicle and those newly resolved on the mind of enlightenment cannot know rightly their coming in and going out. All of these are what is called delusion. Riding on this delusion, they are born according to karma within the three realms and the seven destinies. ...... As the Buddha said: ‘When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.’ Again he said: ‘All lands are held by thought alone.’ When pure thought is accomplished, rebirth is surely obtained; of this there is no doubt at all.”

(The Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra) Modern rendering: Those who are deluded at death are all those who all their lives went along with their wandering thoughts, never cultivating right mindfulness, and their minds were mostly scattered and confused. When the four elements break apart, the deeds of a whole life all appear before them, and their minds tremble with terror and their movements all go amiss. The one who should descend to hell takes the mountain of knives and the forest of swords to be a beautiful garden. The one who should fall among the animals takes the womb of a horse and the belly of a donkey to be a splendid hall. Even those who do good and should be reborn among humans or gods cannot, when entering the womb, escape loving the mother and hating the father so as to be born a man, or loving the father and hating the mother so as to be born a woman. Even the first fruit of the lesser vehicle and the bodhisattvas who have just begun their resolve still have the delusion of the intermediate life between births, and cannot know rightly their entering and leaving the womb. All of these are delusion. Because of this delusion at death, they are born according to karma within the seven destinies of the three realms. ...... As the Buddha said: ‘When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.’ (When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land in which one is born is also pure.) The Buddha also said: ‘All lands are held by thought alone.’ (All lands are wholly upheld by the thought of the mind.) Therefore, when the pure thought of a recitation-practitioner is accomplished, rebirth in the Western Pure Land is surely obtained. Of this, of course, there is not the slightest doubt. [Seven destinies] Hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, spirits, heavens, and asuras. “Destiny” means that toward which one goes. [Buddha-land] The domain that a single Buddha teaches and transforms; there are pure lands, impure lands, reward lands, and dharmakāya lands.

On the principle of the mutual resonance of sympathetic response at the moment of death, Master Yinguang, the incarnation of Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, taught in the Preface to the Guide to Pure Karma for Beginners:

The minds of sentient beings are like water; Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings are complete in faith and vows and, with utmost sincerity, call upon the Buddha, the Buddha responds — just as when the water is clear the moon appears. If the mind is not pure and not utterly sincere, but accords with greed, anger, and ignorance and turns its back on the Buddha, it is like water that is turbid and restless; the moon, though it does not fail to shine upon it, still cannot be clearly imaged in it.”

Rendering: The minds of sentient beings are like water; Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings are complete in faith and vows and call upon the Buddha with utmost sincerity, the Buddha responds — just as when the water is clear and still the moon appears (the metaphor for the pure mind of right mindfulness calling forth Amitābha Buddha's welcome). If the mind is not pure, not utterly sincere, in accord with greed, anger, and ignorance, and opposed to the Buddha, it is like water that is turbid and restless; the Buddha-moon, though it does not fail to shine upon it (the metaphor that Amitābha Buddha is always coming to welcome every being at death), still cannot be clearly imaged there (the metaphor that a restless, turbid mind cannot present the Buddha's welcome, but follows its own wandering thoughts and is reborn according to karma).

Only when the water is clear and still does it appear; when the water is turbid and in motion it is hidden. The moon is surely without preference or rejection; that it does not appear is simply because the water is murky and surging and has no way to take in its reflection.”

Rendering: Only when the water is clear and still does the image of the moon appear; when the water is turbid and in motion, the moon's image does not appear. The moon indeed shines without choosing or rejecting; the reason it does not appear is that the water is murky and surging, so that it cannot bring forth the moon's reflection. (The metaphor: only those beings with right mindfulness at death can see Amitābha Buddha's welcome, while beings without right mindfulness at death cannot see it. Amitābha Buddha indeed welcomes every being at death without choosing or rejecting; the reason those without right mindfulness cannot see him is that their own minds are murky, turbid, and scattered, so they follow their wandering thoughts and are reborn according to their karma.)

Therefore, for the recitation-practitioner, single-minded right mindfulness at death is of utmost importance. A thousand thoughts, ten thousand thoughts, even thinking throughout the whole day and the whole year, is for nothing other than to make ripe this one thought of recitation,
so as to ensure that at the moment of death this thought continues without interruption and calls forth Amitābha Buddha's welcome
. Therefore, Master Shandao and Master Yongming, both avatars of Amitābha Buddha, earnestly teach again and again:
one must accomplish the unbroken succession of ten thoughts at death
(see
the Conditions for Rebirth
This is the word of the sage! If one will not listen to the words of Amitābha Buddha, whose words will he listen to?

[Succession] The thought of recitation following one upon another, unmixed with wandering thoughts. [The measure of the sage's word] This is spoken by the sage, correct and without error, and is certainly to be believed and received.
